REAL DISSENT TO FLAG: Harvard Health credits only the rotator cuff for arm circles (reserving deltoid credit for a different exercise on the same page); a lower-rigor commercial source lists all five muscles. A dissenting clinical view (found via search, not independently fetched/verified) argues arm circles performed in a fixed plane don't meaningfully activate the rotator cuff at all, since true cuff activation needs humeral rotation, not circular swinging. Recommend review before shipping a 'rotator cuff' claim for this specific movement.

sources: Lawrence MA, Chin A, Swanson BT, J Strength Cond Res 2019 (via sci-sport.com summary)
notes: REAL DISAGREEMENT: ExRx's own taxonomy supports reverse hyperextension shifting the target from erector spinae to gluteus maximus. But the one peer-reviewed EMG study found (Lawrence et al. 2019, n=20) found erector spinae/glute max/biceps femoris activation COMPARABLE between standard back extension and reverse hyperextension, with glute/hamstring EMG if anything HIGHER on the standard back extension. State both: ExRx's classification-based claim and the EMG counter-finding, don't resolve.

NASM covers it only in blog posts, not its structured exercise library with Target/Secondary fields. The only EMG-adjacent source found is a 4-subject pilot/methodology study (not a conclusive trial) finding rotational exercises (woodchop-style) actually elicited GREATER deep-core recruitment than anti-rotational (Pallof-style) exercises in that small sample - cutting against the common fitness-media assumption that anti-rotation work is 'more effective' for deep stabilizers. Ship at low confidence or hold back pending a better source.

Covers Russian Twist, Cable/Band Woodchop, Cable Lift, Landmine Rotation, Corkscrew, Suitcase Hold/Side Bend. Genuine, ExRx-documented nuance worth recording: ExRx's own commentary on the standing Cable Twist states 'remarkably little rotation actually occurs through the spine' in a standing position - most rotational force comes from hip rotation, not spinal rotation - while seated/hip-stabilized variants (seated machine twist, ball-supported Russian twist) genuinely rotate the spine against resistance. This is a real distinction worth surfacing rather than flattening all woodchop-family moves into one oblique claim.

Hip thrust muscle list itself is high confidence (direct ExRx page). The 'hip thrust beats glute bridge' claim is NOT backed by a direct head-to-head EMG study - the Contreras 2016 study (J Appl Biomech) compared hip-thrust LOAD VARIANTS against each other (barbell vs band vs American), not against a floor glute bridge; a single-subject (n=1) case study is explicitly anecdotal. Phrase as 'generally understood'/practitioner consensus, not settled fact, per the existing seed research. No standalone ExRx page found for plain glute bridge - treated as the closest equivalent to barbell hip thrust, biomechanically same pattern, lower ROM.

secondary: Gluteus Medius/Minimus (implicated by related clinical literature, not by a stretch-specific study)
sources: https://www.painscience.com/articles/iliotibial-band-syndrome-stretch.php (citing Falvey et al. 2010, Wilhelm et al. 2017, Umehara et al. 2015, Willett et al. 2016, Fredericson et al. 2002)
notes: GENUINE, WELL-SOURCED DISPUTE - do not word this claim as 'stretches the IT band.' The IT band is dense fascia, not contractile muscle. Falvey et al. 2010 (cadaver dissection) found the IT band 'effectively unaffected' by stretching; Wilhelm et al. 2017 found an excised/machine-stretched band elongated only millimeters. The best-sourced position is that the sensation/benefit comes from the TFL (and possibly gluteus medius/minimus, per Ober-test literature) rather than the band itself meaningfully lengthening. Recommend in-app wording: 'targets the TFL/outer-hip region; the IT band itself has limited ability to stretch' rather than asserting IT-band lengthening as fact.

secondary: Obliques (greater on suitcase carry - see notes)
sources: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11042841 (Ellestad et al. 2024, Int J Exerc Sci 17(1):480-490)
notes: CONFIRMED WITH REAL NUMBERS: this peer-reviewed EMG study (18 subjects, surface EMG on rectus abdominis/external oblique/longissimus/multifidus) found Suitcase Carry (unilateral load) produced significantly GREATER contralateral-side activation than Farmer Carry (bilateral load) in all four trunk muscles measured (external oblique +21.9%, p<0.0001; longissimus +15.4%, p<0.0001; rectus abdominis +10.6%, p=0.0068; multifidus +6.1%, p=0.019) - the lateral abdominal wall stiffens the pelvis against unilateral load. The trapezius/forearm-grip 'primary' framing is widely asserted and essentially undisputed in fitness-education literature but was NOT itself the subject of this EMG study (which only measured trunk muscles) and has no ExRx page to cross-check - don't over-state its verification level relative to the trunk-muscle finding. No ExRx page exists for Farmer's/Suitcase Carry at all.

ExRx has no page using the term 'Nordic curl' - closest classified equivalent is 'Self-Assisted Hamstring Raise', explicitly also known as 'Self-Assisted Nordic Raise.' That ExRx variant's upper-body synergist list (pecs/deltoid/triceps/wrist flexors) reflects its specific hand-catch mechanic at the bottom of the fall - a strict Nordic curl or partner-held hamstring lower (no hand-catch) would NOT recruit those upper-body muscles the same way, flagged as a genuine variant difference. Krommes 2021 (n=23) found Nordic curl produces a significantly faster rate of EMG rise in biceps femoris long head than comparable exercises; Hirose 2021 found standard Nordic curls recruit semitendinosus more than biceps femoris long head, with a shallower knee angle increasing BFlh activity. No RCT found linking this EMG activation directly to reduced hamstring-injury incidence in this research pass - don't ship an injury-prevention claim stronger than 'associated with strong biceps femoris long head activation.'

ExRx does NOT classify plyometric/jump exercises with Target/Synergist/Stabilizer muscle fields at all - only joint-action data (hip/knee/ankle extension). Best corroboration is NASM (consistent quad+glute+calf pattern) plus one small EMG study (n=10) that found vastus lateralis (quad) was the most active of the three muscles measured in every jump phase, with gluteus maximus actually the LEAST active of the three - this complicates the common 'glutes are a primary jump mover' framing. Recommend phrasing as 'primarily quadriceps, glutes, and calves working together' rather than asserting a strict ranking.
